newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russian shares hit records as money pours in.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian shares hit records as money pours in.

text.p: Leading Russian shares soared to new peaks on Friday on record volume as foreign investors poured money into Russia, dismissing fears about President Boris Yeltsin's health.
Many of the most liquid stocks rose by more than 10 percent over the day in a highly volatile market.
The Russian Trading System 24-share index rose seven percent to a record 247.69 on record trading volume for the whole market of $58.23 million.
"There is real demand from Western investors, while domestic participants are covering short positions," said Pavel Gronbjerg, co-head of equities at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"But the demand is there. This is a rally."

Moscow power company Mosenergo, which many foreign investors use as a proxy for the whole Russian market, touched $1.53 in afternoon trade then fell back to $1.41, after closing at $1.26 on Thursday. It has risen from below $1 at Christmas.

Another regional utility, Irkutskenergo, jumped over 20 percent to $0.220 in mid-afternoon from Thursday's closing $0.170 after confirming it planned to issue American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) later this month. It later fell back to $0.195.
ADRs allow foreign investors to buy shares while avoiding domestic settlement problems, and Russian companies which have issued ADRs have consistently outperformed the market.
Oil company Surgutneftegaz, which said its ADRs would be launched on Monday, rose to $0.615 after closing at $0.575, off a high of $0.635.
Shares had already hit record levels on Thursday, despite news Yeltsin was admitted to hospital on Wednesday with pneumonia. Doctors said on Friday there had been no breakthrough in his condition.
Share prices were badly hit last year by speculation about the 65-year-old leader's health. Yeltsin underwent heart surgery in November and only returned to the Kremlin on December 23.

But despite Yeltsin's health and other political worries, Russia was the top performing emerging stock market in 1996, with a dollar return of 155.9 percent, and many foreign investors feel they can no longer hold back.
"Mainstream foreign fund managers have started to build substantial stakes in Russia for the first time," said Matt Linsey, emerging markets fund manager for the ING Bank group in Luxembourg.
Equity dealers and analysts said a correction was due after such strong gains. But many said the setback would be only five to 10 percent and quickly lead into a new rally.
United City Bank dealer Dmitry Yevenko said there were already signs of a correction.
"There's a correction on the market. Let's see what happens on Monday. If there's an inflow of new funds, prices will rise again," he said.
Creditanstalt-Grant dealer Andrei Galperin said the launch of Surgutneftegaz's ADRs on Monday could fuel a new rise.
"The most interesting thing is that despite all the forecasts everything is rising furiously," said IK Prospekt dealer Andrei Ippolitov.
"Everyone who could has already sold almost everything but investors are happy to buy at these prices and are even paying a premium," he said.

Treasury bills also advanced, with prices of longer-dated issues rising by half to a full point on Friday, pushing yields down towards 30 percent, in a market which still looks attractive to foreigners, traders said.
